line: Confide settles tokenized stock against a stablecoin in a single transaction, and neither side publishes what moved.

Delivery, and payment, in one transaction — and the only people who can read either number are the two making the trade. Neither side could have happened without the other, which is the only thing a clearing house is for, and there isn't one. Confide holds nobody's assets and stands between nobody.
So why hide it. If you hold tokenized stocks on Solana, everyone can see what you hold. Nobody attacked anything — the chain simply publishes it, the moment each purchase settles.
This is a real account on Solana, right now. The chain says it holds nothing. It holds a hundred and seventy-three thousand shares.
Nearly two thousand of them, from three issuers with nothing to do with each other. Every one leaves the auditor key empty, and every one needs the issuer's signature to open an account.
So I stopped reading the settings and counted. Three hundred and twenty-nine thousand accounts, across Apple, NVIDIA, SpaceX and Anthropic. Not one.
That dollar has the same empty auditor slot and the same locked door. Two regulated issuers, two different asset classes, the same dead end. This was never a story about tokenized stocks.

You cannot do this on one. A pool's reserves are public, and a trade moves them by exactly the amount traded — so anything settled against a pool publishes the size, whatever the token can do. It has to be two parties, directly. That is not a gap here; it is why this is shaped as it is.

The chain will not assemble that trade for you. The proofs do not fit in a transaction, and on a mint that charges a fee one of them does not fit at all. Confide builds them, puts them on chain, and hands each side the other's amount to decrypt before signing. That is the product.

Nobody outside this repository has used any of it. But what is left is not unknown: each obstacle is a condition you can check, and for the two that decide the market, the work on the far side is already running.
